newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Seoul boycotts trade visit to "rude" North Korea.
newsitem.headline: Seoul boycotts trade visit to "rude" North Korea.

text.p: South Korea, miffed by exclusion of its officials from a trip to a North Korean free trade zone, pulled out on Tuesday of a business forum designed to showcase Pyongyang's experiment with capitalism.
The boycott is seen as a major setback to Pyongyang's ambitions to develop the Rajin-Sonbong zone into a thriving, Chinese-style foreign investment window.
It also deals another blow to relations between the two Koreas at a time when Seoul and Washington are groping for a way to attract Pyongyang to the peace table.
Seoul was angered over Pyongyang's rejection of all its officials and journalists who applied to attend the September 13-15 business forum in Rajin-Sonbong. The event is backed by the United Nations.
Pyongyang invited a representative of the Korea Federation of Small Business and 24 businessmen, most from small companies.
Seoul had asked for 53 places, and maintains North Korea agreed to welcome everyone who wanted to attend.

"The arbitrary selection of guests and breach of an internationally publicised promise are unacceptible and the government has decided not to send a delegation," said Kim Kyung-woong, a spokesman for the ministry of National Unification.
"The government thinks it is very rude in international relations for them to arbitrarily select without explanation, standards, reasons or principle," he told a news conference.
Kim suggested the North Korean move indicated a split between military hardliners and more liberal economists over the participation of South Korea.

Pyongyang argued it lacked accommodation, but nevertheless sent invitation letters to officials from China, Japan and the United States. The move is in line with Pyongyang's efforts to bypass South Korea and establish formal ties with Tokyo and Washington.
Western diplomats were at a loss to explain North Korea's decision. Rajin-Sonbong has so far been a failure, and its best hope is to attract South Korean money.
North Korea's foreign trade has collapsed, and it desperately needs investment in export industries to earn hard currency for purchases of food and fuel. The country is on the brink of famine.
"This is a classic case of North Korea managing to find the best way to hurt itself," said one envoy. "Rajin-Sonbong is floundering so far."
North Korea watchers believe a boycott will seriously damage fledgling economic ties between North and South Korea, still technically at war following their 1950-53 conflict.
South Korean businessmen take their lead on North Korean investments from their government, and so far the message has been to risk nothing.
Seoul is uncomfortable with having its businessmen stationed in the North because of worries they could become hostages in a political crisis.

North Korea is dangling 101 industrial projects in Rajin-Sonbong and hoping they will attract $800 million. Among them are a semiconductor plant, oil refinery, naphtha cracker and smaller plants making furniture and toys.

The remote zone lacks basic port and transport infrastructure, and Pyongyang has no money to pay for it. So far the area boasts only two investors -- a Swedish individual and a Chinse shipping company.
